title: THE LESSON I LEARNED FROM JOHANNA
paragraphs: THE LESSON I LEARNED FROM JOHANNA
The Woman Most People Read Past—And the Quiet Faith That Still Has the Power to Change a Life
Most people remember the names that stand at the center of the story.
Peter.
John.
Mary Magdalene.
Paul.
But buried within the Gospel narratives is a woman whose story occupies only a few verses, yet whose example exposes one of the deepest questions of the Christian life:
Will you still follow Jesus when nobody notices?
Johanna did.
And that lesson has haunted me ever since.
We live in an age obsessed with visibility.
People want influence.
Recognition.
Platforms.
Applause.
Credit.
Even in Christian circles, there is a subtle temptation to measure faithfulness by how many people know our names.
But then Johanna appears on the pages of Scripture like a quiet whisper from heaven.
And suddenly everything changes.
The first time we meet her, Luke introduces her almost casually:
“Joanna the wife of Chuza, Herod's household manager.”
The Greek text records her name as Ἰωάννα (Iōanna).
Her name is believed to be connected to the Hebrew idea of God's gracious favor.
And grace would become the defining theme of her story.
Luke tells us:
“These women were helping to support them out of their own means.”
(Luke 8:3)
The Greek phrase is powerful:
διηκόνουν αὐτοῖς
(diakonoun autois)
“they were ministering to them” or “they were serving them.”
This was not passive support.
This was active devotion.
Johanna was not merely attending.
She was investing.
She was sacrificing.
She was participating in the mission of Christ.
And here is where the story becomes astonishing.
Johanna was connected to the household of Herod Antipas.
The same Herod connected to the execution of John the Baptist.
The same political system hostile toward the ministry of Jesus.
Yet somehow, amid power, wealth, influence, and privilege, Johanna saw something greater.
She saw Jesus.
While others chased status, she followed the Savior.
While others served kingdoms that would eventually crumble, she served the King whose throne would never end.
That alone is a lesson our generation desperately needs.
Not everyone is called to stand behind a pulpit.
Not everyone is called to lead crowds.
Not everyone is called to become known.
But every believer is called to serve Christ faithfully.
Johanna reminds us that heaven measures differently than the world.
The kingdom of God celebrates faithfulness long before it celebrates visibility.
And perhaps that is why her story does not end there.
When Jesus was crucified, many scattered.
Fear spread.
Dreams shattered.
Hope appeared buried behind a stone.
Yet Johanna appears again.
Not in comfort.
Not in triumph.
Not when following Jesus was popular.
But when faith cost something.
Luke 24 records that Johanna was among the women who went to the tomb.
Imagine the scene.
Darkness yielding to dawn.
Grief crushing every expectation.
The unbearable silence after the cross.
The confusion.
The heartbreak.
The unanswered questions.
Yet she still went.
The disciples were wrestling with fear.
The future seemed uncertain.
But Johanna kept moving toward Jesus.
Even when she thought He was dead.
That may be the greatest lesson she teaches us.
Real faith continues walking toward Christ even when circumstances make no sense.
Anyone can praise God during abundance.
Anyone can worship during victory.
But what happens when prayers seem unanswered?
What happens when healing delays?
What happens when life breaks your heart?
What happens when the future you expected disappears?
Johanna still walked toward Jesus.
And many of us need that reminder.
Because some people reading this know exactly what it feels like to carry silent disappointments.
The marriage that never became what you hoped.
The child you're praying for.
The diagnosis you didn't expect.
The betrayal you never saw coming.
The loneliness nobody knows about.
The spiritual exhaustion hidden behind a smiling face.
You keep showing up.
You keep praying.
You keep trusting.
Sometimes with tears.
Sometimes with questions.
Sometimes with trembling faith.
But you keep moving toward Jesus.
That is where resurrection stories begin.
The women arrived expecting death.
Instead they encountered life.
The angels announced:
“He is not here, but has risen.”
(Luke 24:6)
The entire Gospel turns on that moment.
And Johanna was there.
Not because she sought recognition.
Not because she wanted her name remembered.
But because faithful people often find themselves standing closest to God's greatest miracles.
That realization changed the way I read Scripture.
Johanna never preached a sermon recorded in the Bible.
She never wrote a New Testament letter.
She never commanded an army.
She never ruled a nation.
Yet God preserved her name forever.
Why?
Because heaven does not overlook faithfulness.
Not one prayer.
Not one sacrifice.
Not one act of obedience.
Not one unseen moment of service.
Not one tear shed in surrender.
The God who sees sparrows sees His people.
The God who numbers the hairs on our heads remembers every act done for His glory.
Perhaps that is the lesson I learned from Johanna.
Your greatest impact may happen in places nobody applauds.
The conversations nobody records.
The prayers nobody hears.
The generosity nobody celebrates.
The faithfulness nobody posts online.
The obedience nobody notices.
Except God.
And His opinion is the only one that ultimately matters.
The Hebrew concept of grace is often connected to the word חֵן (chen), meaning favor, grace, or kindness bestowed by God.
Johanna's life seems to embody that truth.
Grace found her.
Grace transformed her.
Grace sustained her.
And grace positioned her near the empty tomb.
The same grace still changes lives today.
That is the heartbeat of the Gospel.
Not that we climb our way to God.
But that God came down to us through Jesus Christ.
Not that we earned mercy.
But that mercy pursued us.
Not that our failures define us.
But that Christ's finished work redefines us.
From brokenness to redemption.
From shame to forgiveness.
From death to life.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Maybe that is why Johanna's story feels so personal.
She reminds us that ordinary believers are not forgotten in the kingdom of God.
The world may never know your name.
But if you belong to Christ, heaven does.
And that changes everything.
If this message stirred something in your spirit, don't keep it to yourself.
Your testimony may become someone else's encouragement.
If you desire to glorify God through helping truth reach more hearts, your support matters.
The people history forgets are often the people heaven remembers.
